packs.title: Harbour & Parks
packs.promise: Turn Oslo’s waterfront, public collections and parks into discoveries of your own.

q.s: Choose three books for a journey you invent.
st: Invent a small expedition: an afternoon outdoors, a trip through time or a journey to a place you know.
Browse a public shelf and choose a book whose subject would help. Add a second for a completely different job and a third that might surprise your imaginary traveller.
Record each title and its job in your expedition. Use your own words; you do not need to copy any passage or borrow a book.
Return books as the library requests. Choose which one you would take if you could carry only one, and explain the trade-off.

q.s: Turn a waterfront roof into a three-shape composition.
st: From an open public path, find a view of the museum’s curved roof, supporting structure and the water around it.
Choose just three shapes from that view. Draw them on paper or describe their placement, leaving out every detail that is not needed.
Change one shape’s size or position to make a second version. Compare which feels calmer or more in motion, and give your reason.

q.t: A Map with a Point of View
q.s: Decide what your own map should leave out.
st: Choose an old map in the public Map Centre. Read its label and identify what it emphasizes: a coastline, settlements, decoration, routes or something else.
Notice one thing it makes easy to see and one thing it does not show. Treat absence as a design choice you are interpreting, not proof of the maker’s motives.
Make a small map of a familiar place with a purpose of your own: finding quiet, noticing shapes or reaching a meeting point. Use three to five symbols and a simple key.
Name one useful thing you deliberately left out. Your map is an artwork, not directions someone must follow.

packs.title: Along Akerselva
packs.promise: Follow the river into small stories, working buildings and neighbourhood squares.

q.s: Collect shapes that could repeat without a word.
st: From the public square, choose three visible shapes on façades or street furniture. An arch, rectangle, circle or zigzag is enough; you need no particular building.
Compare the shapes by proportion rather than counting every window. Find one tall shape and one wide shape.
Arrange your three shapes into a repeated pattern on your own paper, or describe a six-shape sequence in words.
Look back at the square and name the detail that stops your pattern from being an exact copy of any façade.

q.s: Give an empty stage a tiny wordless scene.
st: View the pavilion from an open public path. Notice how its posts and roof frame the space; you do not need to enter it.
Invent a simple wordless scene with four moments: arrival, discovery, a small change and departure. Use an imaginary character rather than a stranger in the park.
Draw four tiny panels or describe their compositions. Let one real pavilion feature matter in at least two moments.
Give the sequence a final visual detail that connects the first and last frames. No performance or filming is needed.

q.s: Separate what a building shows from what you imagine.
st: From a public street or open riverside path, find three exterior details: a repeated window, a material joint and an opening larger or smaller than its neighbours.
For each detail, record exactly what you can see before guessing what it once helped people do.
Choose your strongest guess and your least certain one. Explain what extra evidence would help you tell them apart.
Finish by identifying one detail that belongs to the building’s present use rather than confidently assigning everything to its factory past.
